# The Manager Effect: Why Leadership Still Matters as AI Saves Time

> **In short:** A new research announcement says the way managers use the time AI saves them can make a difference for their teams. The research looks at the habits of leaders whose employees are thriving. Dropbox's own research names three habits of those managers, and this article explains them and what they could mean for you.

Imagine an AI tool that turns a long meeting into a short summary in seconds. You get back an hour of your week. The real question is what you do with that hour. That question is the focus of new research the company calls "The manager effect."

## What the announcement says

The company behind the announcement says that managers who use AI to save time can shape their teams' experience through what they do with that time. Its research looks at leaders whose employees are thriving, meaning people who are doing well at work and feel supported.

The post, which draws on Dropbox's own internal research, describes three habits of managers whose employees are thriving:

- **They model strong performance and ways of working.** For example, 61% of these managers send follow-up notes after meetings, compared with 43% of other managers, and 61% share meeting agendas in advance, compared with 53%.
- **They reinvest saved time in their people.** They were more than twice as likely to put the time AI saves into coaching, one-on-ones and team development.
- **They stay close to progress without getting in the way.** Among the most senior managers, 92% of those with thriving employees said they understood how their teams were performing against expectations, compared with 74% of other senior managers.

These are one company's numbers from its own workforce, so read them as an example of what to look at, not as a rule for every workplace.

## Why the idea matters

An AI assistant is a tool that drafts, summarizes, or sorts information when you give it a request. It's good at handling repetitive tasks, like writing a first draft of a status update or pulling key points from a long document.

Saved time is only useful if you spend it well. A manager might use it to:

- Check in with a team member who seems stuck
- Prepare for a conversation about career growth
- Listen more in meetings instead of rushing through notes
- Catch up on work that has been piling up

Or the time can quietly disappear into more email. The announcement's central point is that the choice matters, and the choice belongs to the manager.

## A few ways to apply this

These are our suggestions, not findings from the research:

- **Decide your "time back" goal before you start.** Write down one thing you want to do with the hour AI saves each week.
- **Protect the conversations.** Use AI for the paperwork, then keep the one-on-one meetings on your calendar.
- **Ask your team.** Find out which tasks they would like more time for, and which parts of their work they'd rather keep human.

## What this means for you

- **If you manage a team**: Treat saved time as a planning question. Decide what it's for, and check in with your team to see whether they notice the difference.
- **If you work on a team**: Your manager's choices with saved time can affect your day. If you feel more supported or more heard, it may be part of that shift.
- **If you're just getting started**: Pick one repetitive task you already do, such as writing meeting notes, and notice how long it takes. That gives you a starting point for deciding where any saved time should go.

## Wrap-up

The research announcement points to a simple but useful idea: AI can give managers time, and the habits they build with that time can shape how their teams feel and perform. The figures come from Dropbox's own internal research, so treat them as one company's experience before drawing firm conclusions. Your next step is small: this week, write down one task that takes you longer than it should, and one person you'd like to spend more time with if you had that time back.
